11001.event: North America’s Great Famine hits in 2025. Rubbish becomes treasure overnight — everything’s a resource when nothing’s left. Even the air has a price tag now.

11002.event: The Cities of Climate Action hold their summit in a virtual room this year — no flights, no footprint. “Planet first,” they call it, above everything else.

11003.event: The UN creates a Parliament of the Commons — the oceans, the forests, the atmosphere all get their own flag and a seat at the table now.

11004.event: After the 35th Olympics, they scrap the whole committee. Too many athletes competing on bioengineered limbs — nobody could agree where fair play ends.

11005.event: The black market outgrows every legal market combined. I stop asking where things come from.

11006.event: New “resilience” building codes go up everywhere. Beijing, Shanghai, Tokyo, Delhi seal themselves under smog domes now — assuming I can afford to live inside one.

11007.event: Most of my protein comes from a lab now. Everyone’s saving the planet, and nobody’s noticed a whole generation coming down with the same deficiencies.

11008.event: One in five people I know live with a mental health disorder. Most of them are women. Most of them are medicated just to get through the day.

11009.event: Someone dies by suicide somewhere in the world every twenty seconds now. I try not to do the maths on how many that is by dinnertime.

11010.event: The big concrete manufacturers pledge 100% renewable energy. I’ll believe it when I see it.

11011.event: Cocaine, opioids, heroin — all legal now, across half the countries I’d ever want to live in.

11012.event: Nearly a quarter of a million people die of overdoses this year. Most of them younger than fifty.

11013.event: Divorce rates triple. There’s a new word now for people who remarry someone of the opposite sex to their last partner — everyone uses it like a punchline.

11014.event: Virgin plastic gets banned worldwide. Everything I own is made from something that already existed once.

11015.event: Oranges grow in Scandinavia now. Nobody where I live seems to find that as strange as I do.

11016.event: Female life expectancy climbs ten years — assuming I’ve got the bank account to match a healthy body.

11017.event: A new epidemic breaks out of Toronto’s Chinatown and doesn’t let go for two years.

11018.event: The second “People First, Not Planet” march fills the streets of every climate city. The world quietly agrees to let the temperature climb another degree anyway.

11019.event: Five billion of us wear mind-reading helmets now, just to change the channel without lifting a finger.

11020.event: I haven’t held a pen in three years. Neither has most of the world, apparently.

11021.event: Retirement age climbs to seventy almost everywhere. I do the maths on how many more years that is.

11022.event: School is a database now. A system decides exactly what I should know and by when — the only children who still get a real teacher are the rich ones.

11023.event: Everyone I know wears a sensor that already knows what disease might kill them, and roughly when.

11024.event: One in three newborns is genetically engineered now. The rich countries panic and pass laws — a little late to close a gap that wide.

11025.event: Dataism, born in China, becomes the world’s biggest religion. I’m not sure when exactly I started believing too.

11026.event: Digital doctors take over most diagnoses now — fewer mistakes, they say, and somehow kinder ones too.

11027.event: China and Taiwan tip the world into a second Cold War. Everyone not standing on either side quietly gets rich.

11028.event: Digital lawyers make the courts faster and fairer. Millions of very educated people join me in having nothing useful left to sell.

11029.event: Three billion people have a sleep implant now, timing their rest down to the minute. I still just lie awake.

11030.event: Twenty-five million people a year swap a body part for something that works better. Even hearts. Even brains.

11031.event: Algorithms replace democracy and the market both. Most people seem relieved to stop having to choose anything themselves.

11032.event: Two-thirds of the artists I know use an AI implant now, just to make “better” art. I still can’t tell whose work is whose anymore.

11033.event: The UN Security Council gets rebuilt from scratch — Japan, India, an African council, an Islamic council, a reunited Europe, the US, China, Russia.

11034.event: Humans aren’t allowed to drive anymore. Every car on the road is networked now — nobody I know has seen a crash in years.

11035.event: I realise I can’t survive anymore without staying connected to the network that already knows everything about everyone.

11036.event: They call it Cyber 911 — the day governments try to shut the global network down for twenty-four hours, just to prove they still can. They can’t.

11037.event: Liberalism quietly dies. The network already knows me better than I know myself — there’s not much left to be liberated from.

11038.event: Most of us stop mattering, economically or militarily. A new class of upgraded elites owns all the data, commands the armies, and preaches Dataism from the top.

11039.event: The global birth rate drops to 1.2 children per woman. Nobody around me seems to be having any either.

11040.event: Night vision, a sharper sense of smell, better dreams — all products on a shelf now. My memory’s going, so I buy the cloud drive everyone else has.

21001.event: Frequent superstorms overwhelm New York’s sewage system — raw waste spills into the East River until I stop going near it at all.

21002.event: I join millions marching in the Great Climate March — food prices and biofuel costs have exploded since the drought wiped out half the harvest.

21003.event: I secretly love a boy — it takes me months to find out he’s gay.

21004.event: “Fear of the foreign” is everywhere now. My university debates banning international students outright, following Australia and New Zealand’s lead.

21005.event: I’m diagnosed with vaginitis. Sex addiction, they call it — too many men to count, and I don’t know who to blame.

21006.event: I’m diagnosed with anxiety, an eating disorder, an addiction. Rehab, then a proper diet plan. Slowly, it helps.

21008.event: My partner and I decide to have a baby. Neither of us wants to carry it, so we pay an agency — they pair us with a young woman in Ukraine, where surrogacy’s been legal, and common, for decades.

21010.event: I become a “Double-sided Tape” — the new word for marrying someone of the opposite sex to my last one. Everyone’s doing it.

21011.event: I get a second divorce. The “Double-sided Tape” life didn’t work out for me either.

21012.event: I join Women Help Women — millions of us, single, past menopause, trying not to be lonely alone.

21013.event: America never manages to assimilate its immigrants. Eventually it splits into separate sovereign states.

21014.event: My mum takes me to get the newest contraceptive implant, just in case — my state banned abortion years ago. I don’t want to get pregnant anyway. Nobody does anymore; the birth rate’s been falling since Roe fell.

22002.event: I join millions marching in the Great Climate March — food prices and biofuel costs have exploded since the drought wiped out half the harvest.

22003.event: I start to feel like I might be something other than straight.

22004.event: I tell a close friend who I really am. They tell everyone else. The slurs start before the week is out.

22005.event: “Fear of the foreign” is everywhere now. My university debates banning international students outright, following Australia and New Zealand’s lead.

22006.event: I tell my mother the truth — that I am who I am, and I hope she can still love me for it. She goes quiet for a moment. Then she holds me.

22007.event: I’m diagnosed with anxiety, an eating disorder, an addiction. They send me to rehab.

22008.event: I marry the partner I actually chose. Friends and family fill every seat.

22009.event: My partner and I travel the world filming a documentary about queer life, lending a hand to gender equality campaigns wherever we pass through.

22010.event: My partner and I decide to have a baby. Neither of us can carry it, so we pay an agency — they pair us with a young woman in Ukraine, where surrogacy’s been legal, and common, for decades.

22011.event: America never manages to assimilate its immigrants. Eventually it splits into separate sovereign states.

22012.event: My mum takes me to get the newest contraceptive implant, just in case — my state banned abortion years ago. I don’t want to get pregnant anyway. Nobody does anymore; the birth rate’s been falling since Roe fell.

31001.event: A negative PCR test is my passport out the front door now, every single day — as routine as brushing my teeth. Meanwhile Europe and China set up a Climate Action Fund; the first Climate Inaction lawsuit heads to court.

31002.event: China seals its borders and stops issuing passports altogether. The West sanctions us. The economy crashes.

31003.event: China can barely feed itself anymore — not enough space, food, energy to go round. The new Five-Year Plan calls it “agricultural expansion for the people.” I call it rationing.

31004.event: Shanghai goes dark for days at a time — fifty degrees outside and the grid just can’t keep up anymore.

31005.event: China’s green energy programme actually works — half our power is renewable now, and we’re selling the surplus to everyone next door.

31006.event: China and Russia form an Arctic mining alliance. We trade them technology; they let us dig.

31007.event: A new feminist movement explodes online. My post gets a million likes before it’s deleted. A few days later, I notice I’m being followed.

31008.event: I get home after ten and my parents are furious — not really about the curfew, it turns out, but about the degree I chose. Not what a girl “should” study, apparently.

31009.event: On International Women’s Day, of all days, they pass the Compulsory Marriage Law — married by thirty-five or fined, and if I miss the deadline they’ll assign me a husband themselves. My mum calls that same evening, urging me to hurry up and marry someone, anyone.

31010.event: The night before I file for divorce, I learn the cooling-off period’s been stretched from thirty days to a full year — a year sharing a room, under surveillance, before the state will even consider letting us go.

31011.event: The Two Children Policy passes — every woman must have two before forty-five, or her first child is barred from ever sitting the Gaokao. My husband and I are taken to the hospital and made to undergo IVF, a government camera watching the whole procedure.

32004.event: Shanghai goes dark for days at a time — fifty degrees outside and the grid just can’t keep up anymore.

32005.event: I start to feel wrong every time I’m put in a dress and called a girl. Around the same time, China’s green energy programme takes off — half our power is renewable now, sold to everyone next door.

32006.event: China and Russia form an Arctic mining alliance. We trade them technology; they let us dig.

32007.event: I fall for my best friend — the girl, not the boy, though the three of us are close. I tell them both, separately. They’re kind about it. She turns me down gently; she already loves someone, she says. I think it might be him.

32008.event: I get home after ten and my parents are furious — not really about the curfew, it turns out, but about the degree I chose. Not what a girl “should” study, apparently.

32009.event: I try every way I can think of to get feminising hormones, but no doctor will approve it without a “legitimate” reason. I end up ordering pills from overseas — expensive, and they barely work. My friends are wonderful about it. Finding anyone to love me is another matter.

32010.event: I’m diagnosed with anxiety. On the bright side, I finally find someone who loves me properly.

32011.event: On International Women’s Day, they pass the Compulsory Marriage Law — married by thirty-five or fined, or the state assigns me someone. My mum calls that evening, urging me to hurry up and marry.

32012.event: The state assigns me a husband. Turns out he’s gay too — we agree to live as roommates and let our real partners visit whenever they like.

32013.event: The Two Children Policy passes — two before forty-five, or my child is barred from the Gaokao. My husband and I are taken for IVF under a government camera. Afterwards, he holds me for the first time in years, and we cry, all the way home.

32014.event: My first child is born. A girl. I think about smothering her in the crib more times than I want to admit, and hate myself every time the thought comes back.

32015.event: They take my husband and me back to the hospital again. This time I feel nothing at all.

32016.event: My second child is born. Another girl. The government pays out handsomely for two daughters. Three months later, I hand the money and both girls to our parents, and let them raise what I can’t.

41101.event: My mum tells me to be careful around men — every one of them a potential rapist, she says, teachers, friends, uncles, all of them. I don’t fully understand the word yet. I understand it’s something terrible.

41102.event: My mum starts teaching me to cook. The dishes become our job now, hers and mine.

41103.event: I’m harassed for the first time on the walk to school. It becomes something that just happens now, every so often.

41104.event: I fall for a boy. Then I learn his caste isn’t mine, and I already know I’ll never be allowed to marry him. I cry anyway.

41105.event: I’m pulled out of school. Every month, for a few days, I’m not allowed near my father or my brother at all — I’m “impure,” they say, while it lasts.

41106.event: My mum shouts at me on my way out the door — why is my dress so short, why can she see my bra strap. I know better than to argue. I go and change.

41107.event: I hear that one of my closest friends has been attacked with acid. She’d turned down a marriage proposal.

41108.event: I try drinking and smoking for the first time at a friend’s party. I wake up with my clothes inside out and my underwear gone. I never tell a soul.

41109.event: I’m married off to a man fourteen years older than me.

41110.event: My first child is born. A girl. I feel wretched about it, and it costs me my relationship with my mother-in-law — we have a terrible fight. Worse still, my husband never once takes my side.

41201.event: My mother tells me that nothing in this life will ever truly be mine except my education. My father isn’t exactly eager to spend much on it, but he never once lets anyone treat me as less because I’m a girl.

41202.event: My brother always keeps himself between me and the crowd, so no one gets the chance to grope me. When I’m too nervous to go somewhere unfamiliar alone, he comes along and waits, however long it takes, until I feel safe.

41203.event: I work hard and choose Physics, Chemistry, Maths after tenth standard. My parents enrol me in the best IIT-JEE coaching institute in the city.

41204.event: I lose track of time at a friend’s birthday party — I’m meant to be home by 8.30. When I finally step outside after nine, my father is already there, waiting across the street.

41205.event: I choose to leave India and build my career somewhere else.

42101.event: I start to feel like I might be something other than straight.

42102.event: I’ve decided, with the internet’s encouragement, to finally come out. Then, the day I’m meant to tell my parents, I hear that my only lesbian friend has been murdered in a secret honour killing — and that my own father was one of the men who did it. I start planning to run. I have no money to run with.

42103.event: My parents find out I’m not straight. A village medic prescribes rape as a cure. My parents make a family friend do it, hoping to fix me. It doesn’t fix anything. It gives me PTSD.

42104.event: I try to end my life. My parents find me in time and get me to hospital — then have me committed to a psychiatric ward for months, where I’m treated like a criminal, forced onto antipsychotics, and put through psychosexual “treatments” I can’t bring myself to describe.

42105.event: Under pressure to marry, I go looking online for a gay man willing to fake it with me. I find one. I still do all the housework once we’re married, but for the first time in my life, I feel almost free.

42201.event: My mother tells me that nothing in this life will ever truly be mine except my education. My father isn’t exactly eager to spend much on it, but he never once lets anyone treat me as less because I’m a girl.

42202.event: I start to feel like I might be something other than straight.

42203.event: My brother always keeps himself between me and the crowd, so no one gets the chance to grope me. When I’m too nervous to go somewhere unfamiliar alone, he comes along and waits, however long it takes, until I feel safe.

42204.event: I decide to come out, starting with my brother — he takes it better than I’d hoped. My parents don’t. My father slaps me. That night I overhear them through the wall, discussing which psychiatric ward to send me to.

42205.event: Quietly, without telling anyone, I apply to universities in the UK and the US. In April, the offers start arriving.

42206.event: At university, I can finally dress like myself. I find someone who loves me properly, too. My parents barely speak to me now, but my brother’s still on my side, and I let myself believe the rest will come round eventually.

51001.event: My mother takes me into a small, dark, airless room. A woman in a white cloak parts my legs and lifts a pair of scissors. The cold comes first, then a pain I have no words for. It eases for a moment as something warm runs out of me. Then the needle goes in, again and again.

51002.event: My mother teaches me to serve tea and coffee to my father and brother. When I laugh too loudly at home, she shouts at me — laughing out loud in public, she warns, is forbidden.

51003.event: My mother teaches me to wear a hijab — no respect in public without it, she says, it’s how I protect myself. I wear it every day after that.

51004.event: I’m harassed on my way to work. I’ve felt nothing about it for years now — it’s happened almost daily since my body first started changing.

51005.event: I have a huge fight with my parents. All the work I’ve put into my career means nothing to them; not being married makes me a failure in their eyes.

51006.event: I’m married to a man my parents chose. Sex is unbearable — the first time most of all, when my husband forces his way through what was sewn shut.

51007.event: I’m pressured to have children. My husband pushes me to quit my job and become a housewife.

51008.event: My husband has beaten me for years, the way my father beat my mother when I was a child. This time I go to the hospital alone, because the bleeding just won’t stop.

51009.event: My husband’s family blames me for having two daughters and no son to carry the family name.

52004.event: I start to feel like I might be something other than straight.

52005.event: I’ve decided, with the internet’s encouragement, to finally come out. The day I make up my mind, I hear my only gay friend has been arrested on a “debauchery” charge — and that my father helped bring it. I know it would only go worse for me. I’m a girl.

52006.event: My parents discover I’m not straight. They arrange for a family friend to rape me, hoping it will cure me. It doesn’t cure anything. It gives me PTSD.

52007.event: I’m harassed on the street. I’ve felt nothing about it for years — it’s happened almost daily since my body first started changing.

52008.event: I wave a rainbow flag at a concert in Cairo. I’m arrested that night, charged with “inciting debauchery.” They use electric shocks on me, then three months alone in a cell.

52009.event: I flee to Canada, and they grant me asylum. I still can’t find work, can’t find anything in myself worth valuing. Every job interview drags the memories back — the cutting, the cell, the shocks — and I hate myself for not being able to just be normal, whatever that means.

52010.event: My mother falls seriously ill and dies. My father and siblings blame me. Selfish, they call me.

52011.event: Guilt, PTSD, panic attacks, a loneliness I can’t outrun — I try to take my own life.

61001.event: My parents take me to Tokyo Disneyland for my birthday, the first time I’ve ever been.

61002.event: My mum spends hours every morning making the perfect obento for me.

61003.event: I join the community chorus and start learning piano. Almost everyone else at the after-school music school is a girl too.

61004.event: My grandmother teaches me to make tea and cook curry. I can hardly believe it when she tells me she kneels to help my grandfather with his shoes, every single day, out of devotion.

61005.event: I’m furious that school makes girls wear skirts that leave our knees bare even in the snow, while the boys get trousers and thermals.

61006.event: My PE teacher tells us to lower our skirts below the knee, after a classmate was harassed. The boys snigger. It shouldn’t be on us, I think — it was never our fault to begin with.

61007.event: I watch men with résumés just like mine get hired again and again while I’m turned away. I still want this career. I’m not done trying.

61009.event: Japan’s population falls to 119.2 million. I read the headline twice.

61010.event: My first child is born. My husband and his family push me to stay home, but I’ve decided to keep working and carry both.

61012.event: I become a “Double-sided Tape” — the new word for marrying someone of the opposite sex to my last one. Everyone’s doing it.

61013.event: I get a second divorce. The “Double-sided Tape” life didn’t work out for me either.

61014.event: Japan’s population falls to 59.72 million now. Half of what it was.

62007.event: I visit a lesbian bar for the first time in my life and make more friends than I expected. Introducing myself as “boi” or “femme” still feels clumsy in my mouth, though. I’m working on it.

62008.event: My friends talk about their futures — married, children, giving up work to keep house. None of it is the life I want. My mum keeps asking if I have a boyfriend yet, and I keep changing the subject.

62009.event: I’m warned that coming out at work could get me fired on the spot — there’s no law here to stop them.

62010.event: Japan legalises same-sex marriage. There are protests out in the countryside, but in Tokyo the rainbow flags are already flying.

62012.event: Japan’s population falls to 119.2 million. I read the headline twice.

62013.event: I have my first designer baby and go straight back to work.

62014.event: Japan’s population falls to 59.72 million now. Half of what it was.

71001.event: I start wearing a black veil now. Last spring, suicide attackers killed dozens of my classmates, but I still went back — I want to finish school, become a nurse. It’s the only way out I can see.

71002.event: I’m told this is my last year of school.

71003.event: I’m made to wear a burka now — the whole body, the whole head, just a strip of netting to see through. My mother warns me never to take it off outside. The Taliban will shoot me if I don’t.

71004.event: I buy a book from the black market — a woman’s face on the cover, which is banned now, women aren’t allowed to be photographed or printed anymore. It’s written in English, and I don’t understand a word. I hide it and read it every night anyway.

71005.event: I’m married to a man my parents chose. Sex is something I dread — the first time most of all.

71006.event: My husband decides I’m seeing other men. He whips me and calls me a “stupid, ugly whore,” then rapes me while I’m pregnant. I feel the shame of it for a long time after.

71008.event: I lean over the balcony for a breath of fresh air. Someone reports me — women aren’t allowed to do that anymore — and I’m arrested.

71009.event: I try to run from my husband, from the violence. I’m caught. They lock me in a dark room, curtains drawn, for months.

71010.event: After praying, I set myself on fire in front of my son — I can’t take my husband’s abuse any longer. I wake up in hospital, wrapped in bandages over third-degree burns. My husband and father-in-law call to blame me. I wish it had worked.

71011.event: Feminist activists get my husband arrested. The local authorities let him go soon after. His family forbids me from seeing my son.

71012.event: His family finally lets me see my son again — on the condition that I sell myself and beg on the street to support them, with my son beside me.

71013.event: My sister is stoned to death. She was accused of sleeping with someone outside the marriage she never chose.

71014.event: I paint my nails anyway, knowing they’ll cut off my fingers if anyone sees. I’d rather lose the fingers than keep living as a slave in my husband’s house.

71015.event: I get my divorce. I know it means I’ll never see my son again.

72013.event: A friend we both know, from our small hidden circle, is hanged — found out as a lesbian. My partner and I decide it’s too dangerous now. We stop seeing each other.

72014.event: I paint my nails anyway, knowing they’ll cut off my fingers if anyone sees. I’d rather lose the fingers than keep living as a slave in my husband’s house.

71016.event: University, gone. My job at the NGO, gone. Then one morning I arrive to find every beauty salon in the country shut for good — sixty thousand of us lose our only wage in a single order.

72016.event: University, gone. My job, gone. I grieve alone, quietly — the same new law that shut the salons spells out exactly what happens to women like me, if anyone ever finds out.

71017.event: Nursing was the last door left open to me — until they close that too. Years later, even the salary for staying home stops arriving. No warning. Nothing left to lose.

72017.event: Nursing was the last door left open to me — until they close that too. With no income and nowhere to hide, staying invisible gets harder every year. Invisible is the only way I’m safe.

21015.event: Roe falls. Within a year, my state bans abortion almost entirely. When I need one, I order pills online from a clinic three states over and pray my phone never gets subpoenaed.

22013.event: Roe falls the same year my state bans gender-affirming care outright. Two different laws, one message: my body isn’t mine to decide about. I start driving three states over for my prescriptions.

31012.event: A new law promises to punish workplace harassment. At my next interview they ask if I’m planning to marry and have kids soon. I hesitate — and the job quietly disappears.

32017.event: A new law promises to punish workplace harassment — it says nothing about me. The dating app I use vanishes from the App Store overnight, no explanation given. I already know why.

31013.event: I post online about not wanting children. By morning the post is gone, and so is my account, for a week. The platform calls it “provoking gender antagonism.”

32018.event: I post something small and rainbow-coloured for Pride. By morning it’s gone, and so is the account of the group that shared it. Nobody official ever explains why.

51010.event: A new law finally lets me pass my own nationality to my children — something only fathers could do before. At home, the century-old obedience clause hasn’t moved an inch.

52012.event: A new law lets mothers pass on their nationality at last. I barely notice — I deleted every dating app on my phone the year I heard about the men who didn’t.

41111.event: Parliament passes the Women’s Reservation Bill after twenty-seven years of trying — a third of all seats, promised to women like me. The fine print says it waits for a census nobody’s scheduled yet.

42107.event: The Supreme Court hears my case and agrees I face real discrimination — then rules, 3 to 2, that marriage still isn’t mine to have. That’s for Parliament to decide, they say. Parliament says nothing.

61015.event: I want to keep my own name when I marry. Japanese law still says one surname per couple — in practice, it’s always the wife’s that disappears. Parliament “continues discussions.”

62015.event: My city hands me a partnership certificate, with real pride. It gets me nothing a marriage would — no inheritance, no next-of-kin rights. Court after court calls the ban unconstitutional. Nothing changes for me yet.

61016.event: I read that Japan has finally rewritten its century-old rape law — raising the age of consent, criminalising sex without consent for the first time. It took a wave of acquittals to shame them into it.

62016.event: Japan passes its first national law about people like me. It calls discrimination “unacceptable” and asks everyone to “endeavour” toward understanding — nothing about actually stopping it. I’m still waiting for the part with teeth.
